title: Needs, wants, and types of expenses

sections.skill: Classify expenses as needs or wants and as fixed, variable, or periodic

questions.prompt: Ella is building her first budget. Which expense is a NEED for most people living on their own?

choices.text: A premium streaming subscription with no ads
Concert tickets with friends next month
A newer phone model to replace a working one
Groceries for basic meals

questions.intro: A need is something required to live and work: basic food, housing, utilities, transportation to work, and necessary medical care. A want is something that makes life more enjoyable but is not essential. Many items have a need part and a want part: you need food, but restaurant meals are mostly a want.
questions.feedback: Basic groceries are a need. The others are wants, even if they feel important.
questions.topic: Needs, wants, and types of expenses

misconceptions.A: Treats an entertainment upgrade as essential

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Which expense is FIXED (the same amount each month)?

choices.text: Rent of $950 under a one-year lease
Groceries, which change with what you buy each week
Electricity, which changes with the weather and usage
Gasoline, which depends on how much you drive and the price

questions.correct_answer: Rent of $950 under a one-year lease
questions.intro: Fixed expenses stay the same each month, such as rent under a lease or a car payment. Variable expenses change from month to month, such as groceries, gas, and utilities. Periodic expenses happen less often than monthly, such as car registration or yearly fees.
questions.feedback: Rent set by a lease is fixed; the other three vary.
questions.topic: Needs, wants, and types of expenses
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Omar's monthly take-home pay is $2,150. His expenses: rent $875, food $340, transportation $210, phone $55, utilities $120, and entertainment $150. How much is left?
questions.intro: A budget compares income with expenses. Add all expenses, then subtract the total from income. A positive result is a surplus; a negative result is a deficit.
questions.topic: Needs, wants, and types of expenses

misconceptions.C: Gives total expenses instead of what is left

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Omar's phone plan costs $55: $35 is the basic plan and $20 is for unlimited premium data he rarely uses. How should he think about this expense?

choices.text: About $35 is a need and $20 is a want
The whole $55 is a need because phones are essential
The whole $55 is a want because phones are optional
It is neither a need nor a want, because it is a contract

questions.correct_answer: About $35 is a need and $20 is a want
questions.feedback: Splitting a mixed expense shows how much could be cut without losing the essential service.
questions.topic: Needs, wants, and types of expenses

misconceptions.B: Treats the whole bill as essential

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a PERIODIC expense?

choices.text: A $950 rent payment due on the first of every month
A $60 grocery trip each week of the month
A $55 phone bill that is the same every month
A $180 car registration paid once a year

questions.correct_answer: A $180 car registration paid once a year
questions.feedback: Periodic expenses come less often than monthly, so they are easy to forget when budgeting.
questions.topic: Needs, wants, and types of expenses
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

sections.relationship: Classifying expenses requires knowing what income and expenses are.

questions.prompt: Which is INCOME?

choices.text: Pay from a part-time job
A payment for a phone bill
Money spent on a movie ticket
A bank fee

questions.intro: Income is money you receive, such as pay, tips, or gifts. An expense is money you spend or pay out.
questions.feedback: Pay from a job is income.
questions.topic: Needs, wants, and types of expenses
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Which is an EXPENSE?

choices.text: A paycheck deposit
A birthday gift of cash
Interest earned on savings
A monthly bus pass

questions.feedback: A bus pass is money spent: an expense.
questions.topic: Needs, wants, and types of expenses
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Income is $500 and expenses are $560. What is the result?

choices.text: $60 left over to save
$1,060 left over
Nothing, because they cancel out
A $60 shortfall

questions.intro: When expenses are larger than income, the difference is a shortfall (deficit). It has to be covered by savings, borrowing, or spending less.

questions.prompt: Why track expenses for a month before making a budget?

choices.text: To see where money actually goes
Because banks require a month of records first
Because tracking lowers prices at stores
Because expenses are taxed only when tracked

questions.correct_answer: To see where money actually goes
questions.feedback: Tracking shows real spending patterns to build a realistic budget.
questions.topic: Needs, wants, and types of expenses
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

sections.relationship: Money left subtracts total expenses from income.

questions.prompt: Lena tracked one month of spending: food $410, of which $180 was restaurants and delivery. What percent of her food spending was restaurants and delivery (nearest whole percent)?
questions.intro: Tracking spending by category shows where money goes. Comparing a part to its category total, as a percent, helps you decide what to change.
questions.topic: Needs, wants, and types of expenses
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Lena cuts restaurants and delivery from $180 to $100 a month. How much does she free up in a year?
questions.topic: Needs, wants, and types of expenses
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Which tracking method is MOST likely to give a complete picture?

choices.text: Recording every purchase, including cash, for a month
Guessing totals at the end of the month
Reviewing only the largest purchases you remember
Tracking only debit card purchases, not any cash ones

questions.correct_answer: Recording every purchase, including cash, for a month
questions.intro: Small purchases are easy to forget. Apps, bank downloads, receipts, or a notebook all work, as long as every purchase, including cash, is recorded.
questions.feedback: Complete tracking catches small and cash purchases that add up.
questions.topic: Needs, wants, and types of expenses

questions.topic: Needs, wants, and types of expenses

questions.prompt: After tracking, Lena finds she spends $90 a month on subscriptions she rarely uses. What is the best next step?

choices.text: Keep them all, since each one costs under $15
Add one more so she has more choices
Stop tracking, since the amounts are small
Cancel or pause the ones she rarely uses

questions.correct_answer: Cancel or pause the ones she rarely uses
questions.feedback: Rarely used subscriptions are easy savings: $90 a month is $1,080 a year.
questions.topic: Needs, wants, and types of expenses
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Two students each spend $60 a month on the gym. For Kim it supports a doctor-recommended exercise plan; for Lee it is rarely used. Which statement is fair?

choices.text: The gym is always a want for everyone, whatever the reason
The gym is always a need for everyone
Expenses cannot be classified at all
The same expense can be closer to a need for Kim

questions.correct_answer: The same expense can be closer to a need for Kim
questions.intro: Needs and wants depend partly on a person's situation and values. Labeling honestly helps you decide what to protect and what to cut when money is tight.
questions.feedback: Context matters: the same purchase can serve different purposes for different people.
questions.topic: Needs, wants, and types of expenses
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Which budget choice best matches the value "being debt-free"?

choices.text: Paying extra on a credit card balance
Buying the newest phone on a payment plan
Using buy now, pay later for clothes
Taking a cash advance for a trip

questions.correct_answer: Paying extra on a credit card balance
questions.feedback: Aligning spending with values means directing money to what matters most to you.
questions.topic: Needs, wants, and types of expenses
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.prompt: Spending to keep up with friends is called social pressure. Which response protects a budget?

choices.text: Suggesting a lower-cost activity together
Using a credit card so no one notices
Skipping a bill to afford the outing
Spending the same, then cutting groceries

questions.feedback: A cheaper alternative keeps the friendship and the budget.
questions.topic: Needs, wants, and types of expenses

misconceptions.D: Shifts the cost to a need

questions.prompt: A "want" can be planned for. Which approach does that?

choices.text: Buying it now on a store credit card and paying it off slowly
Never buying any wants
Waiting for a refund to pay for it
Saving $25 a month toward a $300 concert trip

questions.correct_answer: Saving $25 a month toward a $300 concert trip
questions.feedback: Saving in advance lets you enjoy wants without debt: $300 ÷ $25 = 12 months.

questions.prompt: Which statement about wants is MOST accurate?

choices.text: A healthy budget never includes any wants
Wants should be paid for with credit
Wants matter more than bills
Planned wants fit a healthy budget

questions.correct_answer: Planned wants fit a healthy budget
questions.feedback: Budgets that include some planned wants are easier to stick to.
